extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, in-house counsel, and practitioners handling or considering ITC Section 337 investigations in the United States
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and procedural/substantive requirements for initiating, defending, managing, and resolving US ITC Section 337 investigations involving patent infringement claims. Covers jurisdictional rules, domestic industry, pleading requirements, discovery, hearings, remedies, Commission review, timing, and strategic considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction and importation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The ITC asserts in rem jurisdiction over accused products (articles) imported into the US; the investigation concerns the accused product, not the accused party. The accused products must be imported into the US for ITC jurisdiction to exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complainant must determine who is importing the accused products and name those importers as respondents. The Federal Circuit has held that the ITC lacks jurisdiction over electronic transmission of digital data into the US (articles limited to material things). Inducement can occur after importation and ITC authority extends to goods used to directly infringe at the inducement of the goods' seller (case citations: Suprema; Comcast).

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic industry requirement (two prongs)
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy domestic industry in a patent case, complainant must demonstrate significant US activity related to at least one claim of each asserted patent (19 U.S.C. § 1337(a)(3)). There are two elements: the economic prong and the technical prong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic prong: requires significant US activities (production/manufacture, R&D, licensing) related to products that practice the asserted patent; quantitative analysis required (Lelo). Technical prong: economic activities must be related to the asserted patent and the patented article must practice at least one claim (Alloc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic industry based on licensing and NPE access
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensing activities can satisfy the domestic industry requirement (allowing non-practicing entities to file) if the licensing relates to each asserted patent and there exist protected articles that practice the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revenue-driven licensing is given less weight. For large patent portfolios, complainant must show sufficient nexus between licensing activities and the asserted patents. Litigation activities related to licensing may count if substantial, relate to a licensing program that encourages product development, and litigation costs are documented (Motiva; InterDigital; Microsoft).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-suit investigation and complaint factual pleading requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Section 337 is a fact-pleading venue, a detailed pre-suit investigation is required and the complaint must contain detailed factual allegations, including claim charts for all patent claims asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigation should analyze importation, domestic industry, and remedy issues. Complaint must include detailed infringement claim charts and contentions, a description (with evidence) of domestic industry, detailed information regarding proposed remedy, and background materials; a separate public interest statement is required. Drafting takes weeks/months and often portions filed under seal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting with the Office of Unfair Import Investigations (OUII) / Staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainant should meet with the Staff (OUII) pre-filing to vet the case and receive feedback on sufficiency of allegations in a draft complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meeting is an opportunity to check importation, domestic industry, and remedy issues, and to assess overall case strength. Developing a good working relationship with Staff is important because Staff (commission investigative attorney) participates as a party and can influence procedural and substantive matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service and institution mechanics; Notice of Investigation (NOI)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complainant need not serve respondents unless requesting temporary relief. If the Commission institutes an investigation, it serves the complaint and publishes a Notice of Investigation (NOI) in the Federal Register describing allegations, parties, and assigned ALJ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NOI sets the actual scope of accused products using plain language; read the NOI carefully to determine the investigation scope and which imported products fall within asserted claims (19 C.F.R. § 210.10(b)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary relief (procedural and substantive tests and timelines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainant may request temporary relief at filing or before institution. Substantively, test mirrors preliminary injunction in district court, but timeline is far more aggressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ID on temporary relief due no later than 70 days after NOI publication for ordinary cases, and 120 days for complicated cases (19 C.F.R. § 210.66(a)). The expedited schedule must include discovery, expert testimony, hearings, and post-hearing briefing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery availability and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: All standard district court discovery tools are available (interrogatories, document requests, depositions, requests for admissions), but with specific ITC limits and accelerated timing (19 C.F.R. § 210.27(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits include maximum of 175 interrogatories per party; complainants as a group may take no more than 20 fact depositions or five per respondent (whichever greater); respondents' group cap of 20 fact depositions (19 C.F.R. §§ 210.28(a) and 210.29(a)). Responses typically due within 10 days; condensed windows (2–3 months) to collect, review, and produce documents. Parties can seek extensions by agreement or court order on good cause. ESI discovery may be limited if not reasonably accessible; privilege procedures for inadvertent production apply. Third-party discovery possible but judicial enforcement may be impractical given time constraints; ITC lacks subpoena authority over foreign persons (19 C.F.R. § 210.32). ALJs are likely to impose preclusion sanctions for gamesmanship (19 C.F.R. § 210.33).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary hearing format and practical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: ITC hearings are similar to district court trials but compressed and without juries; hearings often last 1–2 weeks and may run long hours including weekends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties must present a significant amount of detail in a short time; direct testimony is usually offered through previously written witness statements, leaving the first live substantive testimony often on cross-examination. Hundreds of documents may be entered into evidence. Federal Rules of Evidence are more liberally applied (e.g., hearsay may be allowed). Enormous pressure exists to limit issues tried.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-hearing and post-hearing briefing (waiver consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-hearing briefs must include all evidence and arguments regarding key issues; ALJs will find waiver of any argument not included in the pre-hearing brief (19 C.F.R. § 210.40). Post-hearing opening briefs are due two weeks after hearing; responsive briefs two weeks thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of compressed schedules, pre-hearing and post-hearing briefs are more voluminous and time-intensive (and expensive) than district court counterparts. Parties should prepare exhaustive pre-hearing submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial Determination (ID) requirements and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: ALJ must make detailed findings of law and fact in the ID covering all contested issues and elements of a Section 337 violation. IDs are typically detailed and can exceed 100 pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ALJ must file the ID no later than four months before the Target Date and under typical schedules the ID is due only six to eight weeks after parties file their briefs. Early disposition may be directed on potentially dispositive issues within 100 days of institution (19 C.F.R. § 210.10(b)(2),(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission review and petition for review standards and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may petition the Commission to review an ID on limited grounds; the Commission may decline to review or may review issues de novo and adopt, modify, or reverse the ID (19 C.F.R. § 210.42(h), 210.43).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounds for petition: (1) material fact clearly erroneous; (2) legal conclusion erroneous or abuse of discretion; (3) determination affects Commission policy (19 C.F.R. § 210.43(b)). Petitions for review are due 12 days after service if the ID addresses whether there is a Section 337 violation. Issues not raised in the petition are deemed abandoned before the Commission and on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies available (no monetary damages; exclusion and cease and desist orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ITC cannot award monetary damages. Primary remedies are exclusion orders (limited and general) and cease and desist orders; consent orders may also be entered and enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LEO: limited to products made/imported by or on behalf of named respondents but not limited to specific model numbers; historically provided downstream relief but Kyocera limited downstream relief. GEO: applies to all infringing products and requires showing a widespread pattern of unauthorized imports from many sources (higher standard). Cease and desist orders target domestic respondents with US inventory (19 U.S.C. § 1337(f)). Complainants must plan remedy strategy early; waiting until late in discovery is a common and costly mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic implications of exclusion order types and respondent joinder
rubrics_metrics.description: Because GEOs are harder to obtain, complainants often include many respondents to increase chances of effective relief; joint defense groups and case-management challenges follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complainants must consider naming importers to secure LEOs covering the imported articles and weigh the need for GEO to cover non‑named downstream products. After Kyocera, obtaining relief against non‑named downstream parties via LEO is more difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement and post‑violation remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs enforces exclusion orders; ITC enforces cease and desist and consent orders and may collect penalties in district court. ITC may authorize seizure and forfeiture on repeat violations and levy civil penalties for violations of cease and desist orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties can be up to $100,000 per day or twice the value of the goods, whichever is greater (19 U.S.C. § 1337(f)(2)). The ITC can pursue enforcement proceedings and issue advisory opinions on whether proposed conduct would violate existing orders (19 C.F.R. §§ 210.75–210.79).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction practices and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Most ALJs will consider separate claim construction briefing or hold Markman hearings, but not always; counsel should review ALJ ground rules and past schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim construction is left to the ID after the hearing, all expert reports, summary judgment motions, and evidence must account for all possible constructions. The absence of a Markman stage may delay settlement discussions until near the evidentiary hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case management and client-side resourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the accelerated timetable, parties must immediately identify point persons and allocate client resources to support fast discovery, witness preparation, and expert work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point person(s) should oversee strategy, manage document collection, identify and prepare client witnesses for accelerated schedules, and assist with expert retention and prior art searches. Expect substantial pretrial work, including long witness statements and voluminous exhibits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent procedural responses and defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents must file their response to the complaint within 20 days of service of the NOI (10 extra days for foreign respondents) and compile detailed client information and defenses on an accelerated timetable (19 C.F.R. §§ 210.13(a), 201.16).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents have less time to prepare some defenses (e.g., prior art searches, inequitable conduct); defenses targeting remedies unavailable in the ITC are unhelpful. Counterclaims cannot be litigated within the ITC and must be removed to district court (19 C.F.R. § 210.14(e)). Respondents often consider reciprocal litigation or their own Section 337 filings to gain leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stays and interplay with district court and USPTO proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent has a statutory right to stay co‑pending district court litigation on the same patent until the Commission's determination becomes final (28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)). Stays of ITC proceedings are rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ITC stay motions are evaluated under a multi-factor balancing test considering the state of discovery and the hearing date, whether a stay will simplify issues, undue prejudice, stage of USPTO proceedings, efficient use of ITC resources, and alternative remedies. File stay motions promptly because the factors include the state of discovery and hearing date. ITC has seldom stayed investigations for PTO proceedings and never for pending IPRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early disposition (100-day) program and suitable issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The ITC may direct an ALJ to issue an ID on potentially dispositive issues within 100 days of institution under the early disposition program (19 C.F.R. § 210.10(b)(2),(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues suitable for early disposition include standing, importation, patent exhaustion, and 35 U.S.C. § 101 (subject matter eligibility). Petition for review of such IDs is due five calendar days after service; Commission reviews within 30 days.
